title: Choosing image compression modes and target sizes
description: Compare JPEG/WebP quality and PNG Lossless, Smart, Maximum or Target size. Understand preserved dimensions and when an original stays unchanged.
seoDescription: Choose image modes or a maximum-byte target. Understand PNG lossless and color-reduction modes, preserved dimensions and truthful unmet targets.

body.text: Choose settings for the job you need the image to do. A quality setting changes how a lossy encoder represents detail; a size target sets a maximum number of bytes. The image tools preserve original display dimensions.

body.caption: A qualitative illustration of the size–quality trade-off, not a measured benchmark or a guarantee for a particular image.

body.text: Balanced: a useful starting point

Maximum is the default for images. Balanced is available for JPEG and WebP when you prefer a more moderate quality trade-off. It aims for a practical compromise between encoded size and visible detail. Results depend on the image and its existing encoding, so inspect faces, text, gradients and fine textures at the same scale.
High quality: keep more detail

High quality uses a higher encoding-quality setting. It can preserve more fine detail while providing a smaller size reduction, or none at all. A high setting cannot recover information already lost from the source. The displayed quality value is an encoder control, not a percentage score for visual fidelity.
Maximum: prioritize smaller output

Maximum uses a lower encoding-quality setting for JPEG and WebP. Artifacts can be more visible around lettering, edges and textures. It does not silently resize the image. Keep the result only when the quality is suitable for its intended use.
Target size: a verified maximum in bytes

Target size is a separate mode rather than an option hidden inside Maximum. Choose a preset or enter a custom maximum. Here, 1 KB means 1,000 bytes: a 50 KB limit is 50,000 bytes. The tool measures actual encoded outputs and verifies the final byte count before marking a target as met.

For JPEG and WebP, a bounded quality search keeps the highest-quality candidate it finds within the limit. This is not a mathematical guarantee of the best possible encoding. If the original already fits and no transformation was requested, keeping it avoids an unnecessary lossy generation.

Some limits cannot be reached within the supported quality, dimensions and format. An output over the maximum is marked Target not met. The tool does not pad or truncate a file, quietly resize it, or call a near miss a success. Consider a different format or a less restrictive target.
PNG: Maximum by default, with a Lossless choice

Lossless preserves the decoded PNG pixels and transparency. Smart, Maximum and Target size may reduce colors while preserving transparency values; their color changes can be visible. Dimensions stay unchanged. PNG uses these named modes rather than the JPEG/WebP quality slider.

Smart uses more conservative color-error checks than Maximum or Target size. These checks are numerical heuristics, not a guarantee of invisible changes. Target size measures actual PNG candidates, including color-reduced ones, against your maximum. A lossless result or unchanged original may be retained, and an output above the maximum is marked Target not met.
Original display dimensions are preserved

Image compression and conversion preserve original display dimensions. There is no image resize option. EXIF orientation can be normalized: an upright image may have different stored width and height from the camera file, without changing its displayed orientation.

body.title: When the original is already efficient
body.text: In ordinary same-format compression, a candidate that is not smaller is discarded. The original is returned unchanged with 0% reduction. A requested conversion is reported as a separate transformation and may increase bytes; growth is never presented as a saving.
Apply changed settings to your original

Changing settings does not change an existing download. Choose Recompress to apply the new setup to the retained original, rather than repeatedly encoding a previous result. The previous download stays available until a new run succeeds. Afterward, review the applied setup, output dimensions, quality and actual size before keeping the new result.
Check color, metadata and the actual download

Re-encoding may normalize color to sRGB and remove embedded metadata. That is different from a guarantee of perfect ICC-profile preservation or metadata sanitization. A retained original keeps its bytes and metadata. Compare dimensions, transparency, byte counts and visible detail, and keep your source for future editing.
